title: Who speaks the curses of Psalm 109:6–19: is it the psalmist’s own prayer, or words he reports from his adversaries?
summary: Psalm 109 first speaks of adversaries in the plural (“they”), then of a single man (“him”, “he”) in a series of curses, then of “mine adversaries” again. The verses quoted do not say whether the curses are the psalmist’s own words or words he reports from his adversaries.
text: KJV Psalms 109:2: “For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful are opened against me: they have spoken against me with a lying tongue.” KJV Psalms 109:4–5: “For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer.” “And they have rewarded me evil for good, and hatred for my love.” KJV Psalms 109:6–8: “Set thou a wicked man over him: and let Satan stand at his right hand.” “When he shall be judged, let him be condemned: and let his prayer become sin.” “Let his days be few; and let another take his office.” KJV Psalms 109:16–19: “Because that he remembered not to shew mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, that he might even slay the broken in heart.” “As he loved cursing, so let it come unto him: as he delighted not in blessing, so let it be far from him.” “As he clothed himself with cursing like as with his garment, so let it come into his bowels like water, and like oil into his bones.” “Let it be unto him as the garment which covereth him, and for a girdle wherewith he is girded continually.” KJV Psalms 109:20–21: “Let this be the reward of mine adversaries from the Lord, and of them that speak evil against my soul.” “But do thou for me, O God the Lord, for thy name's sake: because thy mercy is good, deliver thou me.”
reasoning: In the verses quoted, 109:2–5 speak of what “they” have done to the speaker. From 109:6 the verbs and pronouns of the verses quoted are about a single person, “him” and “he”, and the verses quoted from 109:6 to 109:19 are wishes for harm to that person or statements of why it is wished. At 109:20 the speaker refers to “mine adversaries” and to “them that speak evil against my soul”, and at 109:21 turns to ask the Lord to do something for him. The verses quoted do not mark where the curses begin or end as someone’s reported speech, and do not say who the single man of 109:6–19 is. Possible readings: (1) the curses are the psalmist’s own prayer against one adversary among those named in the plural; (2) the curses are the words the adversaries spoke against the psalmist, which he reports before 109:20 answers them; (3) the plural adversaries and the single man are the same people spoken of in two numbers. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. This question is about the verses quoted in this record; it does not say what the rest of the psalm, its title or other books say. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, and does not claim that the psalm is a contradiction.

title: “The Lord said unto my Lord” — who is “my Lord” in Psalm 110:1?
summary: Psalm 110:1 reports one speech by “the Lord” to “my Lord”. The psalm’s own verses quoted do not name the one addressed, and two New Testament passages quote the verse and give an application of their own.
text: KJV Psalms 110:1–2: “The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.” “The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies.” KJV Psalms 110:4: “The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.” KJV Matthew 22:43–45: “He saith unto them, How then doth David in spirit call him Lord, saying,” “The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool?” “If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?” KJV Acts 2:34–36: “For David is not ascended into the heavens: but he saith himself, The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand,” “Until I make thy foes thy footstool.” “Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made the same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.”
reasoning: Psalm 110:1 has two persons, “the Lord” who speaks and “my Lord” who is told to sit at his right hand. In the psalm verses quoted (110:1, 2 and 4) the one addressed is told to sit at the right hand, to “rule thou in the midst of thine enemies”, and is called “a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek”, but no verse quoted gives his name or says whether he is a person then living, a later person, or a role. In Matthew 22:43–45 the question asked is how David calls him Lord, and the passage as quoted does not answer it. In Acts 2:34–36 the verse is applied to Jesus. The record does not say whether those applications settle who the one addressed was in the psalm’s own setting. Possible readings named in the quoted passages: a person David addressed as lord; a person later than David; the one the New Testament passages apply it to.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted. The record does not examine the psalm’s title, other Old Testament passages, or the other New Testament quotations of this verse. It does not decide between readings and does not set the New Testament passages against the psalm. The question of Melchizedek at Psalm 110:4 is a separate published question; 110:4 is quoted here only as context.

title: “When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion” — which turning does Psalm 126:1 recall, and how does it stand to the prayer of 126:4?
summary: Psalm 126:1–3 speaks of a turning of the captivity of Zion as past, and 126:4 prays “Turn again our captivity”. The verses quoted do not say which turning is recalled or whether 126:4 asks for the same event again or for a further one.
text: KJV Psalms 126:1–2: “When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream.” “Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The Lord hath done great things for them.” KJV Psalms 126:3–4: “The Lord hath done great things for us; whereof we are glad.” “Turn again our captivity, O Lord, as the streams in the south.”
reasoning: The first three verses speak in the past: the Lord “turned again the captivity of Zion”, “we were like them that dream”, “The Lord hath done great things for us”. The fourth verse is a request: “Turn again our captivity, O Lord”. The verses quoted do not name the captivity, the time, or the people who were turned, and do not say whether the request of 126:4 is made after the event of 126:1 or in the same breath as a memory of it. Possible readings: the first verses recall a completed return and the request asks that its fulfilment be completed; the request is made by people still in captivity who recall an earlier deliverance; the first verses are a hopeful anticipation put in the past form. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the four verses quoted. The record does not examine the psalm’s title or any other passage on a return from captivity, and does not say that any reading is the right one.
